bib.title: Always-OnAgents:A Survey of Persistent Memory, State, and Governance in LLMAgents

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Always-On Agents: A Survey of Persistent Memory, State, and Governance in LLM Agents", Tianyu Ding, Aditya Nannapaneni, Bingfan Liu, Ling Zhang. arXiv 2606.30306v1 [cs.MA], 29 Jun 2026. Preprint.

COVERAGE: The PDF has 136 pages and 495,867 chars. I did NOT read every page. I read the abstract and TOC, the introduction and contributions, the definition (sec 2.1), the task-ledger state section (3.2.1), organize/consolidation (4.2.3), the context-window substrate (5.2), the checkpoint/rollback substrate strand (5.6), the continual-adaptation "silent entropy" passage (6.4.3), and all of sec 9 (AOEP protocol, pilot, robustness, limits). I grepped the rest for ralph, compaction, progress, handoff and checkpoint, and found no hits on the first two. I did not read sec 7, 8, 10, 11 or the references in full. Page numbers below are printed page numbers; the PDF page is printed+1.

CORE CLAIM: Always-on agents should be treated as persistent-state systems. Each state item is scored on six axes: authority, scope, mutability, provenance, recoverability, actionability. State moves through a lifecycle: observe, write, validate, organize, retrieve, act, update, forget, audit, rollback. The literature concentrates on accumulating and retrieving state more than on governing, recovering or relinquishing it.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
- Rollback is rare. 27 of 435 coded works expose any rollback mechanism. Setup: the authors' own scoped 435-work corpus, not an exhaustive census. p.30.
- AOEP-v0 pilot, 9 fault patterns, 7 systems, local Qwen2.5-7B reader, greedy decoding, deterministic validator. p.84-85.

| System | Obligation pass |
|---|---|
| Governed reducer (oracle upper bound) | 15/15 |
| No-memory floor | 0/15 |
| Naive append | 7/15 |
| Full context | 7/15 |
| Vector-RAG | 7/15 |
| Mem0-style | 4/15 |
| Real mem0ai | 3/15 |

- Reader sweep, full-context system. Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B all score 7/15. Mistral-7B scores 4/15. p.85-86.
- Sampled decoding (T=0.7, top-p 0.95, 5 seeds): obligation pass is 6-8/15, mean 6.6, SD 0.8. p.86.
- Realistic episodes, 3 hand-authored: the reducer passes 9/9, raw stores 4/9, the Mem0-style store 2/9. Real AppWorld traces, 3: the reducer passes 7/7, ungoverned systems 3-6. p.86-87.
- Cited (not the authors' own) results, which I did not verify against the originals:
  - CRAB (Wu et al. 2026) lifts checkpoint recovery correctness from 8% to 100%. p.49.
  - Continuously LLM-consolidated memory rises, then falls below the no-memory baseline (Zhang et al. 2026a). p.57-58.
  - Naive in-context use of recent history beats several purpose-built memory architectures (Asawa et al. 2026). p.57.

ABLATION: None run. The authors propose, but did not run, adding a minimal governance envelope (permission epoch, deletion ledger, trust tier) to an extracted-fact store. Reader-size and seed sweeps are their only robustness checks. Cost and wall-clock are not reported.

QUOTES
- "the sliding window discards old tokens, so the substrate forgets by construction" and "an always-on agent cannot treat a long prompt as durable memory" (p.45).
- "This is the silent-entropy reading of long-run degradation, accumulating disorder that grows with interaction count and is invisible to any metric that scores only the current answer." (p.58)
- "Summarization buys compactness at the price of provenance" (p.37). Closest the paper comes to the compaction question.
- "We did not run the envelope ablation above, so we do not claim to separate an architectural limit from an instrumentation gap." (p.87)

LIMITS
- The pilot is small (9 patterns, 7 systems, 3B-8B local readers, one mem0ai configuration). The authors say it is "not a benchmark" and is not evidence that deployed systems generally fail.
- It does not test frontier models, long-horizon coding agents, or compaction versus context reset.
- It has no cost data and no recovery-cost measurement. They concede rollback cost is not measured.
- The "governed reducer" is a hand-built oracle, so the 15/15 shows the obligations are satisfiable, not that any real system achieves them.
- The paper does not mention Ralph loops, progress files, or session handoff. It never evaluates the practice of externalizing state to files.
- The task-ledger passage (3.2.1) only says ledger state lets an agent "resume a long-running goal after a restart", citing AppWorld and MAGE.
- Corpus counts are the authors' own coding.

BUILDS ON: Tulving 1972 (episodic and semantic memory). Soar (Laird 2012) and ACT-R (Anderson et al. 2004). CoALA (Sumers et al. 2024). For the pilot: Orogat and Mansour 2026 (Governed Evolving Memory), Jung et al. 2026, Kwon 2026, Zheng et al. 2023 (LLM-as-judge, which AOEP deliberately avoids). On context windows: RULER (Hsieh et al. 2024), lost-in-the-middle (Liu et al. 2023), StreamingLLM (Xiao et al. 2023).

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 7 (AOEP evaluation flow, ~p.88) is the only one close to usable. I did not extract its caption. Figure 2 (p.8, three-regime stack) is the other option. Neither is a good fit for note 06.

ASSESSMENT: Mostly off-topic for note 06, and weak as a source for it. It is a memory and governance survey, and it says almost nothing about the session lifecycle, progress files, compaction versus reset, or Ralph loops. At most it supports two sentences:
- (a) The context window is an unreliable and ephemeral state substrate (p.45).
- (b) Accumulated or consolidated state can degrade below no-memory ("silent entropy"; cited, not tested here) (p.58).

Better fits among the 03 notes:
- 02-harness-anatomy, for the state, authority and provenance framing.
- 08-maturity, for the point that rollback and governance are rarely implemented (27 of 435).
- 04-execution-boundaries, for the checkpoint-restore and transactional side-effect material (5.6).

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction was clean. The full text is saved at /tmp/ding.txt if you want the rest read.
